notes.meaning: After the sixth trumpet, there is a pause before the seventh. John sees another mighty angel come down from heaven. The cloud is a sign of God's majesty and of God coming in judgment. The rainbow recalls God's covenant (His binding promise) of mercy to His people, as in 4:3. His sun-bright face and fiery legs echo how Christ looked in chapter 1.

differ.view: The angel is most likely the Lord Jesus Christ himself, veiling a glory too great for human eyes.
Early Methodist teaching holds he is a created angel. He swears by God rather than by himself, and this kind of glory is not too much for a creature.
He is a created angel, perhaps Michael, since Christ does not come down to earth until chapter 19.

notes.meaning: The angel holds a small scroll, and it lies open. This is unlike the large sealed scroll of chapter 5. It holds a smaller part of God's plan, which John is to take in and then pass on. Standing with one foot on the sea and one on the land shows that the angel has power over the whole world. He claims all of it for God.

The angel shouts as loud as a roaring lion. Christ himself is called the Lion of Judah. Then seven thunders answer. In the Bible, thunder often stands for God's voice and His judgment. Psalm 29 speaks of the Lord's voice in the storm seven times. These thunders are solemn ways of making God's mind known.

differ.view: Some older Protestant teachers read this chapter as a picture of the Reformation. In that reading, the seven thunders are the Pope's condemnations sent out from Rome, the city of seven hills.

notes.meaning: John was ready to write down what the thunders said. Then a voice from heaven told him to keep it secret. We are not told what they said or why it was hidden, so guessing is pointless. Some teachers suggest God in mercy held back terrors too heavy for us. It is also a reminder that God's plans hold more than we know, and that eager service must wait for God's direction.

differ.view: Some who read Revelation as mostly future events say the setting suggests the thunders are about the coming bowl judgments of chapter 16, while still warning against guessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars suggest the writer is explaining why he left out a set of 'seven thunders' visions already known among prophets of his day.

notes.meaning: The angel raises his right hand toward heaven. That was the usual way to make a solemn oath, calling on God as witness (Genesis 14:22). The scene echoes Daniel 12:7, where an angel also lifts his hands to heaven and swears.

The angel swears by the God who lives forever and made heaven, earth and sea. The One who created everything can surely finish His plan. His promise is that there will be no more delay. In 6:11 the martyrs were told to wait a little longer. Now the waiting is over.

differ.view: Some older Reformed notes take the old wording 'time no longer' to mean that time itself will end and give way to eternity. Matthew Henry lists this as one possible reading.

notes.meaning: When the seventh angel sounds his trumpet (11:15), God's 'mystery' will be completed. A mystery here means God's plan, once hidden but now made known. It is His plan to save His people and set up His kingdom. The word for 'proclaimed' means 'announced good news.' God told this good news long ago through His prophets. The oath is meant to comfort believers who are suffering.

The same voice from heaven that told John to seal up the thunders now speaks again. It tells him to take the open scroll from the angel's hand. The scene closely follows Ezekiel, who was also handed a scroll from God (Ezekiel 2:9 to 3:3).

John asks for the scroll, and the angel tells him to eat it. Eating it means taking in its message fully, so it becomes part of him before he passes it on. It will taste sweet, because God's word is sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10). But it will turn bitter, because it tells of hard and painful things to come.

John obeys right away, and it happens just as he was told. Receiving a word from God, and learning of His care for His people, was sweet. But the message also told of persecution of the church and ruin on the earth, and that was bitter. In the same way, our joy in Scripture is often mixed with sorrow when we compare it with the world, the church, or our own hearts.

John is told he must prophesy again, which renews his calling. His message will be about many peoples, nations, languages and kings, especially as they affect God's people. This message is meant for the whole world. It has now been put into many languages, including our own.
